content: Measles is a leading cause of death among vaccine-preventable diseases, accounting for approximately 44% of the 1.7 million annual vaccine-preventable deaths in children. Antibiotics have been studied as a potential intervention to prevent complications in children with measles, such as pneumonia, other morbidities, and mortality. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of antibiotics in preventing complications in children with measles. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared antibiotics with either placebo or no treatment. The search for relevant studies was comprehensive, covering databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE up to May 2013. Seven trials involving a total of 1,263 children were included in the analysis. However, the methodological quality of most studies was poor, with only two trials being randomized and double-blinded. There was significant variability in the types of antibiotics used, their dosages, treatment schedules, and the methods used to evaluate outcomes. The pooled data from these studies indicated that the incidence of pneumonia was lower in children who received antibiotics compared to those in the control group. Specifically, 4.1% (27 out of 654) of children in the antibiotic group developed pneumonia, compared to 9.6% (59 out of 609) in the control group. This corresponds to an odds ratio (OR) of 0.35, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.12 to 1.01. However, this difference was not statistically significant. Notably, one trial conducted in 1942, which compared oral sulfathiazole with symptomatic treatment, reported an increase in pneumonia rates with antibiotics. When this trial was excluded from the meta-analysis, the reduction in pneumonia incidence among children receiving antibiotics became statistically significant (OR 0.26; 95% CI 0.12 to 0.60). Antibiotics were also associated with a significant reduction in other complications. The incidence of purulent otitis media was lower in the antibiotic group (OR 0.34; 95% CI 0.16 to 0.73), as was the incidence of tonsillitis (OR 0.08; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.72). However, there was no significant difference in the incidence of conjunctivitis (OR 0.39; 95% CI 0.15 to 1.0), diarrhea (OR 0.53; 95% CI 0.23 to 1.22), or croup (OR 0.16; 95% CI 0.01 to 4.06). Importantly, no major adverse effects attributable to antibiotics were reported in the included studies. The authors concluded that while the review suggests a potential benefit of antibiotics in preventing complications such as pneumonia, purulent otitis media, and tonsillitis in children with measles, the overall quality of the evidence is poor. The studies reviewed used older antibiotics, and there is insufficient evidence to establish definitive guidelines regarding the choice of antibiotic, duration of treatment, or the optimal timing for initiation. High-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to provide more robust evidence and address these unanswered questions.
